item.title: 3D segmentation of brain white matter microstructures from sparsely annotated X-ray Nano-Holotomography data.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
We present a multi-class 3D segmentation framework for white matter (WM) microstructures in large field-of-view (FOV) volumes up to (~ 202 × 202 × 780 µm3) acquired using synchrotron X-ray Nano-Holotomography (XNH) imaging. XNH offers wide FOV, nanoscale resolution, and fast volumetric acquisition. However, manual segmentation of tiny and densely packed WM microstructures it resolves is infeasible at this scale. We implemented an expert-in-the-loop deep learning approach for segmenting long-range axons, blood vessels, cells, and vacuoles from large XNH volumes of monkey brain WM. Our initial model, a 3D U-Net, was trained on sparsely annotated corpus callosum (CC) data, a region with relatively homogeneous axonal structure. High-confidence predictions (p ≥ 0.7) from CC and more anatomically complex fiber-crossing regions were refined by an expert and incorporated into an iterative training process, expanding the segmented dataset sixfold within four iterations. Using the expanded dataset, we investigated multiple well-established 3D convolutional and transformer-based architectures with multiple loss functions in this segmentation context. We evaluated model performance at two complementary scales: voxel-wise across entire XNH volumes and object-wise on 3D segmented objects. All trained models performed strongly across every class at both scales, with average voxel-wise Dice > 0.8. This work presents an enabling segmentation framework for XNH-based neuroanatomy, demonstrating feasibility at large FOVs approaching a single MRI voxel. We show that integrating deep learning with iterative expert refinement substantially reduces manual annotation burden, providing a scalable framework for microstructural mapping in XNH data and a basis for informing biophysical models used to interpret MRI.

item.title: Freezing of gait and cognition are associated with white matter microstructure of the corpus callosum in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Experimental brain research
Freezing of gait (FOG) is a common phenomenon in Parkinson's Disease (PD). People with PD and FOG (PD + FOG) present more severe executive dysfunction compared to those without FOG. White matter (WM) microstructure integrity of the corpus callosum has been implicated in both FOG and cognitive impairments in PD. Executive dysfunction likely contributes to FOG; however, whether FOG severity and executive dysfunction in PD are associated with the same corpus callosum WM microstructure deficits remains unknown. This pilot study aimed to identify associations among FOG severity during turning-in-place (FOG-ratio), executive function, and corpus callosum WM microstructural integrity as measured by fractional anisotropy (FA). Twenty-six subjects with PD + FOG underwent magnetic resonance diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and were assessed for FOG severity (FOG-ratio during turning-in-place) and executive function (Frontal Assessment Battery-FAB). Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were calculated, and Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate correction was applied for multiple comparisons. Results showed that FOG-ratio was negatively associated with FAB scores (r = - 0.59, P = 0.003, corrected). FA in the genu and body of the corpus callosum were negatively associated with FOG-ratio (r = - 0.63, P = 0.001 corrected; r = - 0.48, P = 0.014 corrected) and positively associated with FAB scores (r = 0.45, P = 0.017 corrected; r = 0.41, P = 0.025 corrected). This pilot study shows that quantitative measures of FOG severity during turning and executive function deficits are associated with corpus callosum microstructure.

item.title: Structural Connectivity Differences in Tinnitus and Associations With Severity.
item.description:
The Laryngoscope
OBJECTIVES: (1) To determine structural connectivity between paired brain regions in tinnitus using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging. (2) To correlate structural connectivity in tinnitus with tinnitus severity. METHODS: In this prospective cross-sectional study, 367 subjects were partitioned into four cohorts based on bothersome tinnitus (Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) ≥ 15) and audiometric profile (low- and high-frequency loss). Subjects underwent high angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) to create 246 × 246 structural connectome matrices. The ANCOVA with controlled covariates of age and sex revealed structural connectivity (SC) pairs for tinnitus and hearing loss main effects and their interaction effects. The tinnitus pairs underwent partial correlation analysis using total and subscale TFI scores to assess associations of SC with tinnitus severity. RESULTS: Unique ROI pair connections are identified for tinnitus and hearing loss main and interaction effects. Significant structural connectome edges for tinnitus are in bihemispheric superior frontal, left inferior temporal, and right orbitofrontal cortical areas. The auditory cortex is not involved. SC edges encompass both novel and known anatomical connections. Three of the four tinnitus ROI pair connections have significant correlations with tinnitus severity and tinnitus domain impact. Hearing loss is not a confounding factor in these associations. CONCLUSION: Neuroplastic structural changes related to tinnitus include a wider network that extends beyond auditory cortical regions. Correlation with disease severity measures may identify changes as compensatory or compromised.

item.title: Structural Brain Changes Across the Adult Lifespan: A Volumetric and Cortical Morphometric MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background The adult human brain undergoes continuous structural remodeling, with age-related changes exhibiting marked regional heterogeneity. Quantifying these alterations across anatomical levels is fundamental for delineating physiological structural aging and for providing a reference against which pathological processes may be evaluated. This study aimed to characterize age-related structural brain alterations across the adult lifespan (21–96 years) in neurologically healthy individuals using an automated, multilevel morphometric approach, and to establish a quantitative reference framework for structural brain aging. Methods In this study, T1 weighted magnetic resonance images from 403 adults aged 21 to 96 years were analyzed using an automated brain mapping system. Volumetric measures of tissue components, brain regions, and cortical thickness were obtained, normalized to intracranial volume, and evaluated against age using linear regression models. Segmented regression was additionally applied to each measure to test whether age related change proceeded at a constant rate across adulthood. Results Increasing age was associated with reduced brain parenchymal, gray matter, and white matter volumes and increased cerebrospinal fluid volume. Volumetric decline was more pronounced in the cerebrum than the cerebellum. Among subcortical structures, the thalamus showed the strongest association with age. Cortical thickness decreased preferentially in insular, parietal, and frontal regions, with higher sensitivity observed in motor and premotor areas. Segmented analysis identified a change in the rate of volumetric decline for the whole brain, the cerebrum, cerebral white matter, the cerebellum and the hippocampus, whereas cortical thinning proceeded at an essentially constant rate throughout adulthood. Conclusions Structural changes accompanying brain aging show regionally differentiated patterns across tissue compartments and anatomical regions. These findings indicate that brain aging is characterized by regional differences in structural sensitivity, and in the age at which change becomes evident, rather than by a uniform process.

item.title: MRI Features of Endometrial Hyperplasia With and Without Atypia and Early-Stage Endometrioid Carcinoma.
item.description:
Journal of computer assisted tomography
Objective This study aimed to evaluate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features of endometrial hyperplasia (EH) and stage IA endometrial endometrioid carcinoma (EEC), and to assess MRI findings for distinguishing EH from EEC and for differentiating endometrial hyperplasia without atypia (EHWA) from endometrial atypical hyperplasia (EAH). Methods A total of 304 patients were retrospectively reviewed, including 107 with histopathologically confirmed EH (45 EHWAs and 62 EAHs) and 197 with stage IA EEC, all of whom underwent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 3 months before hysterectomy or biopsy/dilation and curettage. MRI findings were compared across groups. Results The frequencies of small intralesional cysts on T2-weighted (21% vs. 5%) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (19% vs. 4%) images and intraluminal linear structures on T2-weighted (12% vs. 2%) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (23% vs. 5%) images were higher in EH than in stage IA EEC, respectively (P<0.01). Signal intensity ratios on T2-weighted (2.45±1.14 vs. 1.66±0.65) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (0.97±0.27 vs. 0.81±0.22) images, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values (1.29±0.34 vs. 0.84±0.18×10-3 mm2/s) were higher in EH than in stage IA EEC, respectively (P<0.01). When comparing EHWA and EAH, the frequencies of small intralesional cysts on T2-weighted images (31% vs. 13%) and ADC values (1.38±0.34 vs. 1.22±0.33×10-3 mm2/s) were higher in EHWA than in EAH, respectively (P<0.05). Conclusions Several MRI features, particularly ADC values, T2-weighted signal characteristics, small intralesional cysts, and intraluminal linear structures, may aid differentiation of EH from stage IA EEC. Discrimination between EHWA and EAH was modest and requires validation.

item.title: Basal forebrain atrophy links short-latency afferent inhibition to cognition in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease is closely associated with degeneration of the cholinergic system, yet the precise structure-function relationships underlying this link remain incompletely characterized. Short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI) is a widely used neurophysiological marker of cholinergic circuit integrity, but its specific anatomical substrate and relationship to domain-specific cognitive decline are not fully elucidated. This study integrated neurophysiology, structural MRI and cognitive data to characterize the association between cholinergic basal forebrain (cBF) atrophy, SAI and cognitive performance in Parkinson's disease. In this cross-sectional study, we enrolled 119 patients with Parkinson's disease spanning the cognitive continuum from normal cognition to dementia (mean age 63.9 ± 9 years) and 32 healthy controls. All participants underwent assessment of SAI and multimodal MRI for automated volumetry of anterior and posterior basal forebrain subregions and substantia nigra free-water mapping. Cognitive status was classified using the Parkinson's Disease Cognitive Rating Scale (PD-CRS), yielding scores for global cognition and fronto-subcortical and posterior-cortical functions. Regression models and bootstrap mediation analysis were used to examine the SAI-cognition association and decompose it into components shared with and independent of the cBF volume. SAI was reduced in patients compared with controls. Within the PD group, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates, SAI was significantly associated with PD-CRS total (β = -0.19, P = 0.013) and posterior-cortical scores (β = -0.44, P < 0.001), but not with the fronto-subcortical score (β = -0.13, P = 0.103). A mediation analysis identified a significant indirect path from SAI to global cognition through the posterior cBF volume [indirect β = -0.071, 95% confidence interval (CI) (-0.158, -0.013); 42% of the total association], with the residual direct path no longer statistically significant after inclusion of the mediator (β = -0.083, P = 0.260). A significant indirect path through the posterior cBF was additionally observed for the posterior-cortical score [indirect β = -0.061, 95% CI (-0.127, -0.006); 15% of the total association], alongside a substantial residual direct effect (β = -0.36, P < 0.001), consistent with SAI capturing aspects of the cholinergic system relevant to posterior-cortical performance beyond macroscopic cBF atrophy alone. These findings are consistent with SAI reflecting cholinergic circuit integrity linked to cBF structural status. The observed pattern of association, in which the posterior cBF volume captures a substantial proportion of the SAI-cognition covariance, positions SAI as a candidate functional marker for tracking cholinergic contributions to cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease, pending longitudinal validation.

item.title: Limbic circuit alterations in bipolar disorder.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
Introduction This study investigated the spatial and temporal pattern of brain white matter (WM) alterations and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in bipolar disorder (BD). Methods Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 67 BD patients (during manic, depressive, or euthymic phases) and 125 healthy controls (HC) at baseline, and from a subsample of 33 BD patients (in a different illness phase) and 23 HC after follow-up. Analyses of diffusion MRI and resting-state functional MRI were performed to characterise fixel-based metrics in WM and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in BD and HC, as well as across timepoints. Results BD exhibited a spatial pattern of WM alterations characterised by reductions in fibre density and/or bundle cross-section involving fornix and cingulum (major limbic pathways), alongside portions of other tracts, compared with HC. Reduced fibre density in the fornix was associated with intrinsic activity changes involving midbrain, thalamus, and connected fronto-temporal cortical areas within the default-mode network in BD. These alterations showed no significant changes over time or across illness phases. Conclusions These findings converge on limbic circuit alterations and suggest a relationship between structural abnormalities of the fornix and functional changes in intrinsic brain architecture in BD.

item.title: Cognition in 6-17-year-olds with Generalized and Focal Pharmaco-responsive Non-structural Epilepsies and its Correlates on Diffusion Tensor Imaging and Quantitative EEG: A Comparative Observational Study.
item.description:
Neuropediatrics
The study compares cognition and its correlates on diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and quantitative electroencephalogram (qEEG) between generalized and focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies and evaluates behavioral comorbidities. The study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in north India in 20 generalized and 30 focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies in 6- to 17-year-olds. Cognition was tested using Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-IV (WISC-IV) and Stroop test and behavior was evaluated using Childhood Behavior Checklist (CBCL). All the cases underwent DTI and a subset underwent resting and task-based qEEG evaluation. Cognition scores were comparable between generalized and focal epilepsies; however, both showed significant impairment compared with historical controls. On DTI, fractional anisotropy of corpus callosum (body in focal and splenium in generalized) and cingulate cortex (in both) correlated significantly with cognition scores. On resting qEEG, cognition scores correlated negatively with absolute α, δ (focal epilepsy), β and θ powers (generalized epilepsy), and positively with α and δ powers (generalized epilepsy). Performance on task-based qEEG showed negative correlation with absolute delta power in both. Impaired CBCL scores were seen in 25% generalized and 16.7% focal epilepsies. Similar correlates on DTI and qEEG for generalized and focal epilepsies highlight the effect of network model of epilepsy on cognition. The negative correlation of α and β powers with WISC-IV and Stroop scores probably indicates an underlying anxious, tensed, and inattentive state leading to impaired performance in these tests. These cases should be routinely screened for behavioral comorbidities providing a therapeutic target for cognition.

item.title: A staged microstructural mechanism of electroconvulsive therapy: disruption, potentiation, and rewiring.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is among the most effective treatments in psychiatry, yet its mechanism remains elusive. We tested the Disrupt, Potentiate, and Rewire (DPR) hypothesis, a staged model in which transient disruption is followed by neuroplastic potentiation and network reorganization, using densely sampled longitudinal multishell diffusion MRI in individuals with depression receiving ECT and age- and sex-matched healthy controls. MRI was acquired 2 h before (TP1) and after (TP2) the first ECT session, 7-14 days after the last session (TP3), and 6 months later (TP4). Multicompartment diffusion metrics were used to characterize diffusion-signal changes putatively related to edema-related changes (free water), extracellular microstructural complexity (hindered diffusion), and gray matter neurite density as well as white matter microstructural integrity (restricted diffusion). Analyses of 141 MRI scans from 22 individuals with depression receiving ECT and 15 healthy controls revealed two complementary findings. First, ECT increased hindered diffusion and decreased free water, predominantly in right-lateralized gray matter regions, suggesting that the well-replicated gray matter volume expansion following ECT may be more consistent with neuroplastic remodeling than with edema. Second, clinical improvement was associated with increased white matter restricted diffusion, with the most extensive associations and strongest statistical support emerging during the TP2-TP3 interval, after an initial TP1-TP2 reduction. These findings provide in vivo human evidence that ECT engages a staged disruption-rewiring process, offering a unifying framework for understanding how ECT-induced perturbation may evolve into therapeutic brain reorganization.Clinical Trial Registration: NCT04348825.

item.title: Disrupted Event Segmentation in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment: Everyday Memory and Entorhinal Correlates.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Event segmentation-the parsing of continuous experience into meaningful temporal units-supports everyday memory. Although prior research has examined event segmentation and memory in healthy aging and very mild dementia, it remains unclear whether explicit segmentation performance in neuropsychologically characterized amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) is differentially related to distinct components of episodic memory, including immediate and delayed memory for event gist and specific details, and how it relates to broader cognitive abilities and medial temporal lobe integrity. Healthy older adults (HOA) and individuals with aMCI viewed a naturalistic video, completed immediate memory tests, and performed explicit event segmentation during a second viewing. Structural MRI was available for a subset of participants. Compared with HOA, individuals with aMCI identified fewer event boundaries and showed lower agreement with a young-adult normative pattern. Segmentation agreement was associated with memory and working memory/executive composites in pooled analyses; within-group models were nonsignificant, and pooled associations may reflect group differences. After correction for multiple comparisons, lower segmentation agreement was associated with poorer one-day delayed detail recall in the aMCI group. Both groups showed better recognition of non-boundary than boundary objects, and better temporal order memory for across-event than within-event pairs. In the MRI subset, greater left entorhinal cortical thickness was associated with higher segmentation agreement, whereas hippocampal volume and parahippocampal cortical thickness were not. These findings identify altered explicit segmentation performance in aMCI and associations with broader cognitive functioning, delayed memory for event details, and entorhinal cortical integrity, although their causal organization remains unresolved.

item.title: Superior frontal and precentral atlas label contact and naturalistic saccade amplitude across geometric estimators.
item.description:
NeuroImage
We explored whether MRI-derived geometry near the superior frontal-precentral sulcal junction differs between hemispheres and relates to naturalistic saccade amplitude. Structural MRI was available for 38 adults, and 37 had usable eye tracking during movie viewing. We compared two measurements of contact between atlas-defined sulcal regions: the length of their reconstructed shared border and the summed lengths of mesh edges that cross between them. The primary reconstructed-border measure did not provide statistically significant evidence of hemispheric asymmetry or an association with saccade amplitude after correction for the two principal tests. The amplitude estimate was negative (Spearman ρ = -.336; unadjusted bootstrap 95% confidence interval -.566 to -.045; Holm-adjusted P = .084). The crossing-edge measure showed a stronger association, but represents a different geometric quantity. Additional analyses examined mesh resolution, normalization, eye-tracking processing, movie segment, recording quality, anatomical comparison regions, and other saccade characteristics. The additional kinematic associations were nonsignificant after correction. Estimates depended on measurement choices, and regional specificity was not established. The primary analysis therefore did not establish an association between the reconstructed anatomical measure and naturalistic saccade amplitude. This exploratory study illustrates how the definition of an MRI-derived measure can affect brain-behavior results. A nonsignificant result does not demonstrate the absence of an association. Independent anatomical validation and replication with participant-specific functional localization are needed.

item.title: A novel anatomo-functional aphasia screening (D-AFAS) for patients with left-hemispheric brain lesions.
item.description:
Brain and language
Language arises from distributed cortical regions interconnected by white-matter pathways. We aimed to develop an anatomo-functional language assessment for perioperative clinical evaluation. The Dresden Anatomo-Functional Aphasia Screening (D-AFAS) is a time-efficient language assessment comprising 43 subtests that was assessed in 79 patients with left-hemispheric lesions involving the language network. Subtest performance was analyzed in relation to cortical lobe involvement and disruption of major language-related white-matter tracts using diffusion tensor imaging tractography. Primarily expressive subtests such as phonemic fluency, tongue twisters, nonword spelling, and working memory sequences were most vulnerable, whereas predominantly receptive subtests such as phonological and semantic judgment, picture recognition, and word reading were relatively preserved. At the tract level, the lowest AFAS total scores were observed with involvement of the arcuate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. Inferior and middle longitudinal fasciculi showed intermediate effects with selective disorders in naming, semantic-driven tasks and reading. The uncinate fasciculus and frontal aslant tract were associated with more selective deficits like reduced performance in speech initiation and sentence construction in FAT- and unique-naming disorders in UF-involvement. Parietal and insular lesion involvement was linked to greater overall language impairment than frontal or temporal lesions. Comparing all multimodal subtests, linear regression analyses demonstrated strongest associations between AFAS total score and picture description and picture naming. Overall, these findings emphasize the dominant contribution of major white-matter pathways to language function and support the D-AFAS as a structured framework for perioperative network-level language assessment.

item.title: Distributed atrophy patterns link seizures, corticosteroids, and cognition in adults with primary brain tumors.
item.description:
Journal of neuro-oncology
Primary brain tumors are associated with widespread neuropathology, extending beyond the lesion itself and reflecting the broader impact of disease and treatment-related burden, but distributed structural injury is difficult to quantify across heterogeneous samples. We applied normative modeling to characterize these impacts, capturing how individual regional brain structure deviates from expectations on an individual basis across the adult lifespan in patients with primary brain tumors. We studied 90 adults with primary brain tumors. Cortical thickness and subcortical volumes were converted to age- and sex-adjusted z-scores using CentileBrain normative models after manual censoring of tumor, edema, and resection cavities. Cortical and subcortical burden indices were derived as the sum of regions with z < - 1. We related burden indices to clinical variables, lesion size, seizure history, anti-seizure medication, and corticosteroids, as well as to neuropsychological domain composite scores, with multivariable and hierarchical models accounting for age, sex, and lesion size. Cortical burden was higher in patients with larger tumors, seizure history, and corticosteroid use. After age, sex, and lesion size adjustment, steroids remained associated with cortical burden. Greater cortical burden was associated with poorer processing speed and language, while greater subcortical burden was associated with poorer motor performance. Pre-radiotherapy normative burden in non-lesional tissue captures clinically linked distributed atrophy in adults with primary brain tumors. Lesion size and corticosteroid exposure were the most robust clinical correlates of cortical burden, likely indexing not only drug effects, but also greater disease- and edema-related burden that is not fully captured by lesion size or tumor grade. Domain-specific cognitive associations support burden as a candidate marker of structural and functional vulnerability entering radiotherapy. Not applicable.

item.title: Reciprocal 16p11.2 Copy Number Variants Differentially Alter Regional Brain Anatomy and Allometric Scaling
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Reciprocal 16p11.2 copy-number variants (CNVs) confer substantial risk for neuropsychiatric disorders and produce opposing effects on brain size, with larger brain volume in deletion carriers and smaller volume in duplication carriers. Regional alterations broadly parallel this global phenotype, but because regional brain measures scale nonlinearly with brain size, it remains unclear whether regional differences reflect expected consequences of altered brain size, regional anatomy disproportionate to brain size, or fundamental alterations in allometric scaling. We analyzed 285 imaging sessions from 235 participants (49 deletion, 59 duplications, 127 controls) using log-log allometric models to distinguish these possibilities. Brain-size adjustment revealed widespread cortical disproportion in both CNVs, with predominantly reciprocal effects driven by surface area rather than cortical thickness, whereas subcortical structures showed convergent reductions disproportionate to brain size. Strikingly, examining genotype-specific scaling exponents revealed distinct allometric patterns between the CNVs. In duplication, regional differences predominantly reflected fixed shifts relative to brain size. In deletion, by contrast, regional differences more frequently varied with brain size, with substantial exponent deviations affecting 32% of disproportionate cortical regions compared with 12% in duplication. Thus, reciprocal 16p11.2 dosage does not simply shift regional anatomy in opposite directions: duplication largely preserves the normally conserved scaling of regional anatomy with brain size, whereas deletion more extensively disrupts it.

item.title: Functional and Neurotransmitter Organization of Cortical Gray Matter Remodeling During Pregnancy
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Pregnancy is a period of profound neuroplasticity, marked by widespread, spatially heterogeneous reductions in cortical gray matter volume (GMV). Yet, whether this remodeling affects cognition is unclear: subjective memory complaints are common during pregnancy, but objective findings are mixed. Using densely sampled longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) across pregnancy, we examined whether gestational GMV change corresponds spatially with normative maps of cognitive function and neurotransmitter receptors. We analyzed 19 T1-weighted MRI sessions of 1 healthy primiparous woman spanning preconception to 36 weeks gestational age. The GMV change map was annotated using 10 cognitive domain maps comprised of 115 Neurosynth terms and 16 positron emission tomography receptor and transporter maps from healthy adults, using dominance analysis and partial least squares (PLS) analysis with spin tests to account for spatial autocorrelation. Total cortical GMV declined by 4.24%. The 10 cognitive domains accounted for significant spatial variation in GMV change (R 2 adj = 0.16; spin P = .03), with learning and memory (37.7%) and action (27.3%) accounting for the largest shares of explained variance. PLS revealed a shared spatial axis in which learning and memory were associated with smaller GMV reductions while action was associated with greater reductions (spin P = .046). The receptor and transporter maps also accounted for significant spatial variation (R 2 adj = 0.22; spin P = .02). PLS identified a significant neurochemical pattern (spin P = .009), with greater GMV reductions in regions rich in cholinergic (VAChT) and noradrenergic (NET) markers and smaller reductions in regions rich in serotonergic, GABA A , and muscarinic M1 receptors. This receptor-derived pattern was positively associated with social function and negatively associated with action. Together, these findings provide new evidence that pregnancy-related GMV remodeling is organized along functional and neurotransmitter receptor axes, suggesting that maternal brain plasticity is a targeted process that may support selective cognitive adaptation.

item.title: Microstructural Analysis of Language Pathways' Development in Term Neonates
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding the early development of language pathways is essential for elucidating how neonatal brain organization supports the acquisition of linguistic skills. In this study, we investigated microstructural changes in term human neonates scanned at postmenstrual ages (PMA) of 37 to 44 weeks. Using diffusion MRI data from 310 healthy infants in the developing Human Connectome Project, we employed q-space diffeomorphic reconstruction to map major language tracts involved in language processing. Fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and other diffusion-based biomarkers were quantified in pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus, extreme capsule, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. Our results revealed significant weekly differences in microstructural integrity across these tracts, with particularly robust age-related reductions in mean and radial diffusivity. In addition, we observed leftward asymmetries in multiple language pathways, suggesting that hemispheric specialization emerges by this early postnatal stage. Although PMA at scan predicted the most pronounced shifts in diffusion metrics, sex showed minimal impact on developmental trajectories. These findings highlight the rapid and tract-specific organization of language-relevant connections during the first weeks of life, providing normative data against which atypical patterns can be evaluated. More broadly, this work offers new insights into the foundation of language circuitry in neonates, informing future studies of neurodevelopmental disorders and potential early-life interventions.

item.title: Socioeconomic disadvantage alters developmental patterning during fetal cortical maturation: evidence from structural covariance network analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with differences in child neurodevelopment that are detectable in utero. Existing fetal imaging work characterizes these differences in terms of tissue volumetry. However, fetal brain development also hinges on tightly regulated spatiotemporal patterning which, if disrupted, can alter long-term neurodevelopment. A cohort of 213 typically developing fetuses underwent fetal brain MRI between 20 and 38 gestational weeks. Cortical thickness was estimated across 78 regions and used to construct structural covariance networks within overlapping gestational windows. We used the Child Opportunity Index (3.0) as a measure of socioeconomic disadvantage. Population-wide development was characterized by significant gestational age-related decline in global density (β = −0.038, p = 0.002) and global synchrony (β = −0.022, p = 0.001). Nodal degree distribution broadened from leptokurtic to platykurtic, consistent with a transition from globally synchronized to segregated and localized growth. The Low COI group showed an attenuated decline (adj R² = 0.21) and a greater dispersion around the fitted model than the High COI group (adj R² = 0.54) in global density. Low COI fetuses showed delayed emergence of architectural hubs, spatially restricted to primary sensory and motor cortical regions alongside slower cortical thickness accrual in seven hub regions. Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with the synchrony and spatial organization of cortical maturation in-utero.

item.title: Within-person ovarian hormone variation and structural connectome topology: a three-visit diffusion MRI study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Ovarian hormone variation has been associated with brain tissue measurements, but whether it accompanies changes in global structural network topology remains uncertain. We analysed 22 naturally cycling participants from OpenNeuro ds005360, with serum measurements and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging during menses, estimated ovulation and the mid-luteal phase. Longitudinal anatomical processing, anatomically constrained tractography and SIFT2 weighting yielded 66 connectomes with 84 nodes. Four primary mixed models tested within-person estradiol (E2) or progesterone (P4) associations with total-weight-normalized global efficiency and modularity Q, adjusting for participant-average hormone concentration, visit order and motion. No association survived four-test false-discovery-rate correction. The largest estimate was negative for E2–efficiency (standardized β = −0.132; 95% confidence interval − 0.258 to − 0.006; p = 0.0398; q = 0.159). Its participant-cluster bootstrap interval excluded zero, but permutation q = 0.111 also exceeded the corrected threshold. The negative direction persisted across participant omissions and alternative graph definitions, but 9 of 22 omissions gave p ≥ 0.05. Secondary global, nodal and connected-edge analyses yielded no corrected discovery. These findings provide no multiplicity-corrected evidence of a hormone association with the tested global topology measures. They do not establish structural invariance. The E2–efficiency direction warrants independent evaluation with larger samples and denser longitudinal measurements.

item.title: Quantitative Resting-State Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Reveals White Matter Network Reorganization in Older Adults With White Matter Hyperintensities
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background/Objectives: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are important imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease in older adults and are closely associated with cognitive decline. However, WMH burden alone cannot fully explain interindividual differences in cognitive impairment. This study constructed white matter resting-state functional networks based on the multimodal white matter atlas (MWMA) and investigated WMH-related alterations in network topology and their associations with cognitive function. Methods This single-center cross-sectional study included 171 older adults, comprising 50 participants with absent or mild white matter hyperintensities and 121 participants with moderate-to-severe white matter hyperintensities. All participants underwent three-dimensional T1-weighted imaging, T2-FLAIR imaging, and resting-state BOLD-fMRI. WMH grading and segmentation were performed using T2-FLAIR images. White matter network nodes were defined using the MWMA atlas, and 173 cerebral white matter regions of interest were retained. Individual 173 × 173 white matter functional connectivity matrices were constructed. Graph-theoretical metrics were calculated across a sparsity range of 0.05–0.50, and area under the curve values were used for statistical analysis. Group differences were assessed using general linear models adjusted for age, sex, years of education, and mean framewise displacement. Exploratory partial correlation analyses were performed in participants with complete cognitive data. Results Both groups retained small-world organization. Compared with controls, the WMH group showed increased aγ and aσ, whereas aEglob, aEloc, and aLp did not differ significantly. The WMH group also showed increased DMN-SMN inter-module connectivity, without significant intra-module differences. Nodal abnormalities were spatially heterogeneous: increased aBc was mainly located in WMH-affected regions, whereas abnormal aDc and aNe were more often distributed in normal-appearing white matter. Several abnormal nodal metrics were associated with TMT-A, TMT-B, and MoCA performance. Conclusions Moderate-to-severe WMH is associated with white matter functional network reorganization rather than complete topological breakdown. These alterations may contribute to WMH-related cognitive decline, particularly impairments in processing speed and executive function.

item.title: Structural and resting-state functional brain alterations in male smokers: a combined voxel-based morphometry and functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Nicotine & tobacco research : official journal of the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco
Introduction Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that chronic smoking is associated with gray matter volume (GMV) reductions and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) abnormalities. However, these changes have largely been investigated independently, and the relationship between regional GMV alterations and corresponding rsFC changes remains poorly characterized. Integrating structural and functional metrics may enhance understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying nicotine dependence. Methods We recruited 51 male smokers and 52 age-matched healthy controls. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify regions with significant GMV differences between groups. These regions were subsequently used as seeds for seed-based whole-brain rsFC analysis. Results Compared with controls, smokers exhibited significantly reduced GMV in the bilateral fusiform gyrus, left temporal pole (TP), and right inferior occipital gyrus. Smokers also showed enhanced rsFC within multiple circuits, including the left fusiform gyrus-right TP, left TP-left inferior frontal gyrus, and right fusiform gyrus-left rolandic operculum, whereas rsFC between the right fusiform gyrus and left insula was significantly decreased. Correlation analyses revealed that left TP GMV was negatively correlated with smoking duration and cumulative tobacco exposure (pack-years). Furthermore, rsFC strength between the left fusiform gyrus and right TP was negatively correlated with both the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND) and DSM-5 tobacco use disorder severity scores. Conclusions These findings suggest that chronic smoking is associated with concurrent GMV reductions and rsFC alterations within visual, social cognitive, and sensorimotor networks, with the left fusiform gyrus-right TP connectivity showing potential relevance to the severity of tobacco use disorder.

item.title: Neonatal white matter volume and latent preschool neurodevelopmental phenotypes in very preterm children.
item.description:
Pediatric research
Background Very preterm children often develop co-occurring cognitive, motor, attentional, and behavioral difficulties. We aimed to identify preschool latent neurodevelopmental phenotypes and examine whether neonatal total cerebral white matter (WM) volume was associated with a multicomponent adverse phenotype. Methods This single-center longitudinal cohort included very preterm children with preschool follow-up at 4-6 years. Latent class analysis (LCA) was based on five binary indicators: IQ < 85, motor risk, and clinically relevant internalizing, externalizing, and attention problems. Neonatal MRI at term-equivalent age quantified total cerebral WM volume. Logistic regression examined the association between standardized WM volume and adverse phenotype membership, adjusted for total brain volume, gestational age (GA) at birth, postmenstrual age (PMA) at MRI, and sex. Results Among 74 children with complete preschool data, LCA identified a low-risk phenotype in 51 children and a multicomponent adverse phenotype in 23 children. The adverse phenotype showed higher frequencies of cognitive impairment, motor risk, and clinically relevant internalizing, externalizing, and attention problems. Among 72 children with neonatal imaging, higher WM volume was associated with lower odds of belonging to the adverse phenotype after adjustment for total brain volume, GA at birth, PMA at MRI, and sex (OR 0.29, p = 0.048). Conclusion Neonatal total cerebral WM volume was associated, in adjusted analyses, with a preschool multicomponent adverse phenotype after very preterm birth. Neonatal brain measures may help characterize multidomain neurodevelopmental vulnerability after very preterm birth. Impact This study identifies a multicomponent adverse preschool phenotype in very preterm children, characterized by co-occurring cognitive, motor, attentional, and behavioral difficulties. Lower neonatal total cerebral white matter volume was associated with this adverse phenotype after adjustment for brain size and perinatal factors. Combining neonatal MRI with person-centered neurodevelopmental phenotyping may help identify very preterm children who warrant closer surveillance and early intervention.

item.title: Biotin intake and mental health: findings from a large population-based cohort and biological insights from hippocampal and gut-brain pathways.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
The relationship between biotin and mental health remains largely unexplored. Leveraging data from the UK Biobank prospective cohort, we found that dietary biotin intake in the second quartile was associated with a 15% lower risk of major depressive disorder, while intake in the third quartile was associated with a 14% lower risk of anxiety disorder, compared with the lowest quartile. Furthermore, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses revealed nonlinear associations between dietary biotin intake and both outcomes, with the lowest risks of incidence observed at biotin intake levels of approximately 40-50 μg. Neuroimaging analyses further revealed positive associations between dietary biotin intake and fractional anisotropy in the cingulum-hippocampus tract, suggesting a potential link between biotin intake and white matter microstructure in a pathway involved in emotional regulation. We then examined the effects of a 9-week biotin intervention in mice and observed changes consistent with two potential pathways: a hippocampus-related pathway involving enhanced protein biotinylation, reduced neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) expression, and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression, and a gut-brain axis pathway characterized by greater microbial diversity and an increased relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, which was positively associated with brain 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) levels. These findings provide complementary biological evidence that may help explain the observed association between dietary biotin intake and mental health.

item.title: Linking Theory of Mind and Cardiac Vagal Regulation: the Integrative Role of the Posterior Cerebellum.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Interpersonal interactions are fundamentally regulated by Social Cognition, a multifaceted construct encompassing the cognitive and neural processes used to navigate the social environment. Within this overarching architecture, Theory of Mind (ToM), or mentalizing, provides a foundational dual-level framework of implicit and explicit systems. Although these functions traditionally rely on a cortical mentalizing network, recent findings support a cerebellar contribution to ToM processes. Given that the cerebellar computational architecture is suited for the rapid, automated processing of visual social cues, investigating lower-level social decoding offers a unique window into the cerebellar contribution to ToM. Building on this framework, the present research explored the relation between cerebellar morphometry and lower-level ToM in healthy subjects. Participants underwent MRI to assess cerebellar Gray Matter volumes and completed the computerized version of the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET). Since the lower-level mentalizing is closely tied to complex interactions between the Central and Autonomic Nervous Systems (ANS), the present study also examined the relationships between cerebellar volumes and Heart Rate Variability, namely the variations of Root Mean Square of Successive Differences (RMSSD) values across the RMET procedure. Findings revealed that volumes of cerebellar lobules VI, VIIb, Crus II, and vermis IX predicted the RMET accuracy. Furthermore, the volume of vermis IX selectively predicted RMSSD variation during the rest-recovery transition, with smaller vermis IX volumes associated with a sharper, more progressive RMSSD decline. Overall, these data highlight that posterior cerebellar morphometry is associated with RMET performance and cardiac vagal regulation, thus supporting lower-level mentalizing.

item.title: Pathogenic mechanism of exacerbated brain atrophy in Alzheimer's disease exhibiting co-pathology of TDP-43.
item.description:
Brain research
While most Alzheimer's disease (AD) which is associated with Limbic Predominant Age-related TDP-43 Encephalopathy (LATE) exhibits accelerated brain atrophy, the pathogenic mechanism remains undefined. In this Perspective, we offer a feed-forward model of TDP-43 dysfunction linked to tauopathy that underpins such exacerbated neuron loss in AD with the co-pathology of TDP-43. Since TDP-43 dysfunction may be initiated in some central neurons of the aging human brain, we modeled this aspect of the human pathophysiology by ablating the gene encoding TDP-43 in excitatory neurons of the mouse forebrain and crossbred them to a tau-seeding mouse model. We found that such selective loss of TDP-43 function facilitated the pathological conversion of endogenous tau to accelerate tauopathy, resulting in exacerbated neuron loss. Since endogenous tau is a substrate of caspases, our finding that TDP-43 dysfunction activated caspase 3 could account at least in part for such an impact on tauopathy. Surprisingly, in our tau-seeding mouse model with deposition of Ab plaques, TDP-43 proteinopathy occurred during late-stage of disease, the emergence of which is dependent on tauopathy. We propose a novel mouse model of AD with the co-pathology of TDP-43 and discuss the potential use of such model to clarify disease mechanisms, disclose novel targets, and to test therapeutic strategies designed to attenuate proteinopathies of tau and TDP-43.

item.title: MoCA deficits and white matter in Huntington's disease.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
This study explored the relationship between the Montreal Cognitive Assessment's (MoCA) subdomains and white matter changes in Huntington's disease (HD). Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were measured using Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) in 22 early-stage symptomatic HD patients and 20 healthy controls. Tract-Based Spatial Statistics was used to compare the two groups and to correlate patients' FA and MD values with their performance on MoCA subdomains. Among all MoCA subdomains, only visuospatial performance was associated with white matter integrity in the corpus callosum, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, supporting the utility of identifying regional imaging correlates of specific cognitive performance through the combination of DTI analysis and brief screening tools in early-stage patients.

item.title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Neurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. Methods We collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. Results We replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. Conclusions These results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

item.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

item.title: Executive functioning as a cognitive-motor bridge in older adults at risk of cognitive decline: Design and baseline findings of the MOVE study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background The MOVE (Maintaining Overall cognitiVE and physical functioning in at-risk older adults) study is a randomized controlled trial investigating whether executive function and motor training can promote cognitive functioning and mobility in older adults at risk of cognitive decline. This study aimed to characterize the relationships among executive functioning, prospective memory, mobility, and brain structure in the study cohort. Methods Ninety adults aged ≥ 60 years with subjective cognitive decline, early mild cognitive impairment, or both were enrolled in the MOVE randomized controlled trial. Before intervention, participants underwent cognitive, affective, prospective memory, and sensor-based motor assessments, including gait, Timed Up and Go, and postural sway. Structural MRI was available for 32 participants. Baseline profiles were compared among participants stratified according to their level of executive functioning, and associations between executive functioning, motor performance, prospective memory, and regional brain volumes were examined. Results Higher executive functioning was associated with better prospective memory, lower fall risk, and more efficient gait and functional mobility. Hippocampal volume was consistently related to prospective memory performance although right cerebellar cortex was involved in remembering to perform an intended action at a specific time. Regional brain volumes across cerebellar, hippocampal, striatal, and parietal regions were associated with gait and functional mobility. Executive functioning significantly mediated the associations between bilateral cerebellar and right striatal volumes and motor performance. Conclusions Executive functioning emerged as a potential link between prospective memory, mobility, and cerebellar integrity, providing a framework for the longitudinal evaluation of cognitive and motor training effects.

item.title: Multimodal neuroimaging fusion with interpretable deep learning for speech motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
PLOS digital health
Speech motor dysfunction affects approximately 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), but multimodal neuroimaging models for prediction of this impairment remain limited. We developed MCTA-FusNet, an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion MRI to predict speech motor dysfunction in PD. The model incorporates modality-specific encoders and a hierarchical triple-attention fusion mechanism to capture channel-, spatial-, and modality-level interactions. Using cross-domain transfer learning, MCTA-FusNet was first pretrained on the PPMI dataset (n = 400) to predict motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) and then fine-tuned on the FAH-SYSU dataset (n = 81) to predict speech motor dysfunction, indexed by vocal response magnitude (VRMag) to pitch perturbations. MCTA-FusNet outperformed all unimodal and multimodal models with transfer learning, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (1.388 ± 0.62) and highest correlation between predicted and observed VRMag (r = 0.731, p < 0.001). Interpretability analyses identified the superior temporal gyrus, primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, and supplementary motor area as key predictors, with greater coherence and phase synchrony between auditory and premotor regions significantly correlated with exaggerated VRMag. These findings establish a multimodal neuroimaging deep learning model for predicting and explaining speech motor dysfunction in PD, offering a novel framework with potential for symptom-specific monitoring and therapeutic intervention.

item.title: Poorer inhibition and switching are associated with lower white matter fibre density in the superior longitudinal fasciculus in groups clinically at-risk of probable Alzheimer's disease dementia.
item.description:
Journal of neurology
Executive dysfunction and white matter microstructural alterations in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) may occur in the clinically defined at-risk groups of Alzheimer's disease (AD) dementia and be potentially useful and early markers of risk. We used diffusion-weighted MRI and fixel-based analysis to investigate inhibition/switching executive functioning and white matter properties of three SLF subdivisions (SLF 1, SLF 2, SLF 3) in groups clinically at-risk of AD-dementia: controls (C; n = 35), subjective cognitive decline (SCD; n = 60), single-domain amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI; n = 55), and multiple-domain amnestic MCI (mMCI; n = 52). Individuals with probable AD-dementia (n = 27) were also compared with controls. Linear trend analyses showed increasingly poorer executive functioning performance and lower fibre density (FD) in the right SLF 2 and bilateral SLF 3 across groups. Analysis of covariance (age, sex) revealed SCD and mMCI groups had lower FD bilaterally in the SLF 3 than controls. The AD-dementia group showed more extensively reduced FD in four of the six SLF divisions, and lower fibre density cross-section (FDC) in five of the six SLF divisions than controls. Partial least-squares (PLS) analyses showed that poorer executive functioning, but not processing speed, was associated with lower FD in the SLF in the at-risk sample. This pattern was also found in AD-dementia/controls PLS, which additionally showed this association with FDC. Collectively, our results implicate altered microstructural fibre properties in the SLF and poorer executive functioning in groups at risk of AD-dementia, with FD changes in SLF present in SCD, prior to objective cognitive decline.

item.title: Regional cortical thickness differences between progressive and stable mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Experimental brain research
Accurately differentiating progressive mild cognitive impairment (pMCI) from stable mild cognitive impairment (sMCI) may help characterize individuals with different patterns of cognitive progression toward Alzheimer's disease (AD). This 24-month MRI study aimed to compare regional cortical thickness and hemispheric asymmetry between the pMCI and sMCI groups. A total of 40 participants, including 20 with sMCI and 20 with pMCI, were selected from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. For each participant, baseline and 24-month follow-up T1-weighted MRI scans were analyzed. Cortical thickness measurements were performed using FreeSurfer software, and bilaterally averaged regional cortical thickness values were analyzed using ANCOVA to assess group differences in baseline-adjusted follow-up cortical thickness, asymmetry, and laterality indices. To correct for multiple comparisons, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied at an FDR of 0.10. The pMCI group exhibited significantly lower baseline-adjusted follow-up cortical thickness than the sMCI group in the inferior temporal, middle temporal, parahippocampal, and fusiform gyri. No significant between-group differences were observed in the Asymmetry Index or Laterality Index. Overall, these findings suggest that regional cortical thickness may provide useful information on structural differences between pMCI and sMCI, particularly in temporal regions.

item.title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

item.title: Individualized Atypicality of Structure-Function Configuration Marks Subthreshold Depression in Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Subthreshold depression (StD) in adolescence represents a critical state preceding major depressive disorder, yet its neurobiological substrates remain poorly characterized. Conventional structure-function coupling rely on DTI tractography, which produces non-isomorphic matrices and unstable single-subject estimates, limiting their clinical utility. We developed a novel isomorphic and multi-omics framework to quantify individualized structure-function configurations and tested whether adolescents with StD show reproducible deviations from a group-mean reference in a validation sample. Methods We integrated five structural (cortical thickness, mean curvature, sulcal depth, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) and five functional (ReHo, ALFF, CBF, local and global connectivity strength) features to construct regional SIND-FIND configurations using symmetric KL divergence in a discovery-validation design (N = 131). Individual typicality scores were defined as the correspondence between each participant’s regional configuration profile and HC reference (Leave one out). The score has undergone parallel validations using conventional SC-FC coupling, molecular alignment (PET/AHBA), and behavioral correlations. Results Group-mean configuration maps were spatially correlated across samples (ρ = .93, p spin < .001). StD participants showed lower typicality than HC (F (1,94) = 8.73, p = .004); the conventional SC–FC comparison was not significant (F (1,92) = 3.31, p = .072). Regional differences involved frontoparietal and salience regions and aligned with PET (r = .55, p spin < .001) and AHBA (r = .47, p spin = .003) maps. After covariate adjustment, typicality correlated with SCL-90 (ρ = −.262, q = .013), SDS (ρ = −.234, q = .022), ISI (ρ = −.296, q = .012) and PSQI (ρ = −.288, q = .012; BH-FDR across five scales); coupling tracked depressive but not sleep symptoms (ISI ρ = −.161, q = .124). Within validation StD participants, SCL-90 remained negatively associated with typicality (ρ = −.42, p = .023). Conclusion Our isomorphic, multimodal framework captures coordinated structures-function deviation in adolescent StD with greater group-effect sensitivity than conventional SC-FC coupling, together with regional specificity, molecular spatial alignment, and behavioral relevance. Configuration typicality, defined relative to an HC group-mean reference, may serve as an individual-level marker of organizational deviation during adolescence, pending larger, demographic stratified samples.

item.title: Spatially localized racial differences in the association between white matter hyperintensities and verbal memory in cognitively unimpaired adults
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are common in aging, but whether their cognitive associations differ between African American and White older adults is unclear. We studied 5,187 cognitively unimpaired non-Hispanic African American (NHA) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) older adults across three independent cohorts using depth- and lobe-resolved WMH mapping with cross-sectional, longitudinal and machine learning analyses. In the Emory Healthy Brain Study (EHBS), greater WMH burden was more strongly associated with poorer verbal memory among NHA than NHW participants. A similar difference was observed in a 34-center cohort but not detected in the third cohort. Differences localized to frontal juxtacortical and parietal deep white matter in EHBS and the multicenter cohort, respectively, and did not parallel WMH burden distributions. Estimates changed little after adjustment for cohort-specific Alzheimer’s disease (AD) biomarkers, vascular risk factors, structural imaging measures and APOE genotype. Accounting for neighborhood deprivation in EHBS yielded a similar estimate. Generalized random forests supported these differences without assuming a linear interaction. Baseline frontal juxtacortical WMH burden showed a stronger association with subsequent AD-signature cortical thinning among NHA than NHW participants in EHBS, with directionally similar multicenter findings. Spatially resolved WMH measures may help identify early heterogeneity in vascular contributions to cognitive aging.

item.title: The Inferior Parietal Lobule Links Childhood Trauma to Non-Suicidal Self- Injury via Anxiety
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) refers to deliberate self-harm without suicidal intent, and the neural mechanisms underlying disturbed bodily self-consciousness (BSC) in NSSI remain unclear. This study examined cortical thickness across BSC-related regions and their mediating role in the childhood trauma–NSSI relationship. Methods A total of 173 young participants (aged 10–24 years) were classified into NSSI (n = 117) and non-NSSI (n = 56) groups based on DSM-5 criteria; structural MRI data with complete surface-quality metrics were available for 128. Cortical thickness was measured bilaterally in five BSC regions: inferior parietal lobule (IPL), supramarginal gyrus, insula, postcentral gyrus, and posterior cingulate cortex. ANCOVA with permutation-based inference and FDR correction, serial mediation analyses with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals, and an exploratory whole-cortex analysis across 34 regions were conducted. Results Only the IPL exhibited significant group differences after FDR correction (p = 0.010, pFDR = 0.049; d = − 0.42), with the NSSI group displaying thinner cortex; in the whole-cortex analysis, the IPL showed the largest cortical thinning of all 34 regions. Childhood trauma correlated with thinner IPL (r = − 0.19, p = 0.039). Serial mediation revealed a significant indirect pathway from childhood trauma to NSSI through IPL thickness and anxiety (indirect effect = 0.012, 95% CI [0.001, 0.040]); the anxiety-alone pathway was more substantial (34.3%), and full mediation was observed. Conclusions Among the five BSC regions, only the IPL was associated with NSSI. Altered higher-order body representation may constitute a neural pathway linking early adversity to NSSI through heightened anxiety.

item.title: Anterior Cingulate Cortex Metabolism, Microstructure, and Social Withdrawal in Autism Spectrum Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) supports social behavior, which can be normalized by manipulating ACC function in animal models of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). How ACC metabolism and microstructure jointly relate to social behavior in humans with ASD remains unclear. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy measured glutamate (Glu), glutamine (Gln), lactate (Lac), and myo-inositol (Ins), while neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging estimated neurite density index (NDI) and orientation dispersion index (ODI) in the same ACC voxel in 96 adults with ASD and 63 typically developing controls (TDC). Analyses included group comparisons, partial correlations, networks, and permutation-based dimensional models incorporating Japanese Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ-J), 25-item Hikikomori Questionnaire (HQ-25), and diagnosis, plus an ASD-only sensitivity analysis using the validated HQ-25 cutoff. ACC Lac was higher in ASD, but the difference was not significant after multiple-comparison correction; Glu, Gln, and Ins did not differ significantly between groups. Four network edges were retained in ASD, with bootstrap support for Glu–Ins and Gln–Lac; none were retained in TDC. Glu correlated significantly with lower NDI and higher ODI only in ASD. HQ-25—but neither AQ-J nor diagnosis—showed significant positive associations with Lac, Glu, and Gln. The ASD-only sensitivity analysis corroborated the Lac association. Altered ACC metabolic–structural coupling in ASD, possibly reflecting astrocytic dysfunction, may be informative beyond concentration differences alone. Metabolite associations with social withdrawal, independent of general autistic traits, suggest a behavioral dimension relevant to precision medicine in ASD.

item.title: Adiposity in Adolescence has Detrimental Effects on Developing Brain Structures and Organization, Communication, and Controllability of Resting-State Networks
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Adiposity in adolescence can have detrimental effects on neural maturation, and is associated with incompletely understood alterations in brain structures and circuits. To address this important knowledge gap, N = 3,341 youth from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) two-year follow-up cohort (median(IQR) age = 12.0(1.1) years; 51.0% females), with structural MRI and resting-state fMRI were studied. Topological properties reflecting network strength, resilience, efficiency and modularity, information transfer, regional feedback costs associated with controllability of network dynamics, and morphometric characteristics were examined as a function of body mass index (BMI), body roundness index (BRI), overweight, obesity, and persistent excess BMI (across assessments). Youth who slept less, spent more time on electronic devices, were Hispanic and/or from lower-income families had higher BMI/BRI (β = 0.07–4.95, 95%CI=[0.03,7.05]), and higher odds of overweight or obesity (aOR = 1.01–1.72, 95%CI=[1.01,2.28]). Higher BMI/BRI, overweight, obesity and/or persistent excess BMI were associated with weaker and less resilient networks supporting decision-making, control, emotional regulation, reward processing and social function (β=-0.11 to -0.01, CI=[-0.16,-0.01]), and more topologically fragile thalamus and basal ganglia (β = 0.05–0.10, CI=[0.01,0.14], p < 0.03). They were also associated with lower control costs in cognitive and topological hubs (including the precuneus and prefrontal regions) that play central roles in regulating brain dynamics, aberrant information transfer in limbic, frontoparietal, salience, somatomotor and cerebellar regions, and lower thickness and/or volume of distributed (including prefrontal) regions, and functional hubs (β=-0.14 to -0.02, CI=[-0.18,-0.01]). Thus, adiposity in adolescence is associated with widespread structural and alterations of brain networks supporting developing cognitive processes, and fundamental mechanisms that control these networks’ dynamics.

item.title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
item.description:
Nature biomedical engineering
Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

item.title: Development of subcortical nuclei volume in utero over the second and third trimester.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Subcortical nuclei are important structures in the brain. Previous MRI evaluation of fetal brain development mostly focused on cerebral cortex and the myelination process, but few of them explored the developmental pattern of subcortical nuclei. The aim of this study is to analyze the developmental characteristics of fetal subcortical nuclei and their relationship with gestational age and cortical development. In this retrospective study, the precise axial, sagittal, and coronal views of T2-weighted brain MRI sequences in 47 fetuses with normal brains in the gestational age (GA) range of 22 to 36 weeks were obtained. A single 3D motion-corrected high-resolution brain volume was reconstructed from the 2D SSTSE imaging stacks using a slice-to-volume reconstruction (SVR) method. The volumes of the subcortical nuclei, i.e., amygdala, caudate, pallidum, putamen, hippocampus, subthalamic nucleus, thalamus, and cortex were segmented and corrected based on the above 3D images. We drew the developmental curve of each subcortical nucleus with age. The Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between volumes of subcortical nuclei, as well as between volumes of cortical and subcortical regions, to explore how cortical regions and subcortical nuclei matured cooperatively. We illustrated the developmental trajectory curves of volumes of six subcortical nuclei and one of subcortical structure (thalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, caudate, putamen, subthalamic nucleus, and pallidum) according to the changes in GA to show the development trajectory of subcortical nuclei at 22-36 weeks. We further illustrated that volumes of subcortical nuclei and subcortical structure increased nonlinearly with GA, and the velopmental trajectories indicated laterality in the subcortical nuclei of the fetal brain. In addition, we found insignificant maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei and cortical regions, whereas the degree of maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei was relatively high. We found the volume of subcortical nuclei increased nonlinearly with the increase of GA, and the trajectory of nuclear mass development was lateral. The patterns of nuclear cluster development could expand our understanding of the brain growth. Reference ranges of fetal intracranial structures across gestational ages can serve as a valuable adjunct to prenatal counseling when interpreted in conjunction with clinical context and ultrasound findings.

item.title: Influence of regional white matter lesion volume differences related to cardiorespiratory fitness on cognition in healthy older adults.
item.description:
GeroScience
Greater cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) has been associated with reduced global burden of white matter hyperintensity (WMH) lesions, a neuroimaging marker of small vessel cerebrovascular disease, and lower risk of age-related cognitive impairment and dementia. However, little is known about how CRF relates to regional patterns of WMH volume and the associated impact on cognitive aging. In a cohort of 166 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (mean age = 70.49 ± 9.96 years, 48.8% women), we investigated the association of CRF with regionally distributed WMH burden using multivariate regional network analysis of hemispheric lobar WMH volumes. We additionally evaluated the moderating role of CRF-related regional WMH volumetric differences for cognition. Higher CRF, distinct from self-reported habitual physical activity, was associated with a distributed covariance pattern of WMH volume reductions in bilateral frontal and right parietal lobes, with relative increases in bilateral occipital lobes. Greater CRF-WMH pattern expression was associated with younger age and male sex. Additionally, there was a significant age-by-CRF-WMH network pattern interaction for memory, but not for information processing speed and executive functioning, such that the higher the pattern expression, the weaker the inverse association between age and memory performance. Our findings suggest that having greater CRF may help to maintain cerebrovascular health in older adults as reflected in its association with reduced WMH burden in regions particularly vulnerable to brain aging and associated memory dysfunction. Multivariate CRF-WMH pattern expression may provide a marker of cerebrovascular health that may help to identify those at increased risk for age-related cognitive impairment.
